name: hypersonic-rANS
baseline: FSE (Finite State Entropy, tANS), FSE Huff0 (Huffman), htscodecs rANS (scalar/SSE/AVX2/AVX-512); also TurboANX (closed source)
workload: Single-threaded decode of enwik8 (100,000,000 bytes) and Silesia x-ray, order-0 static, blocks as in the repo benchmark harness.
claimed_speedup: enwik8 decode: rANS32x64 16w 11 (raw) 3,018.02 MiB/s vs FSE 966.58 MiB/s (about 3.1x, derived from page data), FSE Huff0 2,515.23 MiB/s (about 1.2x, derived), htscodecs rans32avx2 order-0 2,374.04 MiB/s (about 1.27x, derived). Ratio 64.48 % vs FSE 63.2 % and Huff0 63.4 % (slightly worse ratio). README: 'Fastest decoders can reach a throughput of up to 3.3 GB/s'.
compiler_and_flags: clang++ (version and optimisation flags not stated in README; premake5 'releaseclang_x64' config)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, 32 GB DDR5-6000 CL30, Windows 11 via WSL2
tradeoffs: Decode-optimised; every best decoder variant needs AVX2 (some AVX-512 variants), x86-64 only. Encoders are scalar and unoptimised (about 230-350 MiB/s). Needs many interleaved streams (32 or 64 lanes), so small inputs and multi-symbol-per-state formats differ from FSE. Author calls it R&D, not finalised, not integration-friendly yet.
caveats: Ratio and speed trade-offs are per variant; the headline row is the 'raw' mode with slightly worse ratio. TurboANX (closed source) is within about 2% of the top row (2,964 vs 3,018 MiB/s). Compiler version and flags not stated; TurboANX numbers come from a TurboBench run of Jun 2023 on a native Windows build, so mixed environment. Project benchmark, so first-party. Interactive graph page on github.io was not opened (blocked). Last commit is a dependabot-style actions bump.
found_via: WebSearch 'rANS entropy coder SIMD github C++ faster than FSE Huffman benchmark' and github.com/topics/rans page; README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: PIVCO-Huffman (pivco-huffman)
baseline: huf0 (zstd's Huffman decoder, X1 single-symbol and X2 double-symbol variants); also Oodle Huffman (oo-huff) and a traditional 4-stream table Huffman
workload: Decode of a 4M-symbol Huffman-coded block sequence repeated 100 times (400M symbols per run), 5 runs, median of 3 best; synthetic distributions (proba80, flat, zipfian, ...) and real files (html_wiki, english, json_api, source_c, ...).
claimed_speedup: Apple M4 Max: proba80 15,339 MB/s vs huf0 X2 2,617 (5.91x best-of-others); real text 4.3-4.8 GB/s, 2.0-2.5x huf0_x2; Xeon 6975P-C AVX-512: english 7,909 vs huf0 X2 1,875 (4.22x), html_wiki 4,765 (2.96x), proba80 22,581 (11.70x). Encoded size within 1-4% of traditional Huffman.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.5.0 on Amazon Linux 2023 (x86 Xeon and Graviton 4); CMakeLists adds -Wall -Wextra -O3; Apple M4 compiler not stated in the pages opened
hardware: Apple M4 Max (NEON); Intel Xeon 6975P-C AVX-512 VBMI2 (AWS c8i, 2 vCPU); AWS Graviton 4 Neoverse V2; Zen 3 SSE/AVX2
tradeoffs: Not a drop-in: new bitstream (PivCo partition bitmaps), block-based (4096-8192 symbol blocks), encoder walks the Huffman tree; needs SIMD with permute/compress primitives (NEON, AVX-512 VBMI2, AVX2). Encoded size 1-4% above traditional Huffman. PHA variant adds FSE/ANS coded bitmaps for better ratio on skewed data at lower decode speed.
caveats: README marks the project as WIP and not production-ready; co-authored with an AI assistant per commit trailers. Zen 3 SSE/AVX2: README says 0.94-22.5x, three deep-real-text rows lose by about 6%. flat_M7 and some rows are only 1.3-1.4x. In-memory microbenchmark of decode only; huf0 uses 128 KB chunks while PIVCO uses its own block size. Paper (PDF on github.io) was not opened (host blocked); numbers taken from repo docs. Linked arXiv 2606.05765 not opened.
found_via: WebSearch 'fast Huffman decoder SIMD AVX2 github library faster than zstd Huff0 benchmark'

name: sserangecoding (SSE 4.1 interleaved range coder)
baseline: Finite State Entropy (FSE) demo by Yann Collet (tANS) and its Huff0 mode; length-limited Huffman; Fabian Giesen's SSE 4.1 interleaved rANS (ryg_rans)
workload: Order-0 decode of book1 (Calgary corpus, 768,771 bytes), 8-bit alphabet, 16 interleaved 24-bit range-coder streams.
claimed_speedup: Decode 577.1-619.1 MiB/s (2.3-2.5 cycles/byte) vs Collet FSE 370.3 MB/s decode (about 1.6x, derived) and vs ryg_rans interleaved SIMD rANS 512.8-565.6 MB/s on the same machine (roughly 1.1x, derived). FSE Huffman mode (-h) decodes faster: 800.9 MB/s. Output 436,229 bytes vs FSE 437,232 and 16-bit length-limited Huffman 438,385. README: AVX-2 port with 64 streams 1,373 MiB/s.
compiler_and_flags: Tested with clang v10 and gcc v9.3.0 per README; build flags (cmake default) not stated
hardware: Core i7 1065G7 (Ice Lake, about 3.9 GHz); also quotes 4 GHz Skylake and Ryzen 5 3450U
tradeoffs: Decoder is SSE 4.1 and relies on fast vectorised single-precision division with 24-bit integers (precision loss under 1%). Encoder is slower (51.9 MiB/s vectorised, 137.5 MiB/s plain) because of a byte swizzle step and is not optimised. Order-0 only, 8-bit alphabet. Range coding avoids ANS patent concerns (author's argument).
caveats: Single file (book1), single machine, first-party. FSE and Huff0 comparison binaries were not built with identical flags documented. The same README admits FSE Huffman mode (800.9 MB/s) and its own AVX-2 variant are faster than the SSE 4.1 range coder; so it is faster than FSE/tANS and ryg_rans only. Last commit over 3 years ago.
found_via: WebSearch 'rANS entropy coder SIMD github C++ faster than FSE Huffman benchmark' (result snippet), then README via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: FiniteStateEntropy (FSE and Huff0)
baseline: zlibh (the Huffman encoder inside zlib, as packaged by Frederic Kayser)
workload: Compression and decompression of generated probability-distribution files (Proba80, Proba14, Proba02, made with the repo's probagen), 32 KB blocks.
claimed_speedup: Proba80: Huff0 1350 MB/s decode and 600 MB/s encode vs zlibh 300 / 265 MB/s (about 4.5x decode, 2.3x encode, derived); FSE 440 / 325 MB/s with ratio 8.84 vs 6.38 for Huffman and zlibh. Proba14: Huff0 860 vs zlibh 250 MB/s decode. Proba02: Huff0 555 vs zlibh 210 MB/s decode.
stars_or_usage: 1.5k stars; FSE and Huff0 are the entropy stage of zstd
tradeoffs: FSE is a table-based tANS coder (precise like arithmetic coding, but slower than Huff0); Huff0 is Huffman with 4-stream interleaving, loses ratio on skewed distributions (cannot go below 1 bit per symbol). Both are block-oriented with a header describing the distribution.
caveats: Benchmark is old (GCC 4.8.4, Broadwell laptop) and only synthetic generated distributions. Baseline zlibh is a weak Huffman. Better modern Huffman decoders exist (see PIVCO-Huffman and hypersonic-rANS entries). zstd itself (facebook/zstd) is on the known list; this entry is the standalone upstream FSE/Huff0 repo, whose dev branch last changed 2024-03-10.
found_via: WebSearch 'github.com topics entropy-coding rans range-coder C++ library benchmark vs FSE' and direct README

name: htscodecs (rANS 4x8, 4x16, 32x16 SIMD codecs)
baseline: htscodecs scalar rANS 4x8 order-0/1 and its adaptive arithmetic coder (arith); fqzcomp and bsc listed for completeness
workload: Encode and decode 10 MB of NovaSeq quality values (also 10 MB Illumina HiSeq quality values) with rANS order-0/1, with/without RLE and bit-packing.
claimed_speedup: NovaSeq order-0 decode: r32x16 AVX-512 (c0404) 2,098.6 MB/s vs scalar r32x16 (c0000) 613.9 MB/s (about 3.4x, derived), vs r4x8 scalar 718.3 MB/s (about 2.9x, derived) and arith 86.3 MB/s (about 24x, derived). Bit-packed order-1-style: r32x16-o132 AVX-512 3,947.9 MB/s vs 1,861.9 scalar.
stars_or_usage: 40 stars; used by htslib / samtools CRAM
tradeoffs: Format-specific (CRAM 3.1 codecs), interleaved 32-way rANS stream needed for SIMD; runtime CPU dispatch. Gather-heavy AVX2/AVX-512 paths were affected by Intel GDS/Downfall microcode mitigation (README notes simulated gather can be faster on patched systems).
caveats: Numbers are one data type (quality values), one machine, compiler and flags not stated; README says figures are 'purely a snapshot'. The comparison is mostly SIMD vs scalar within the same library, plus its own arithmetic coder, rather than an outside incumbent. LICENSE.md says BSD for most files with some listed exceptions (c_range_coder.h and rANS_byte.h/rANS_word.h are public domain). Also appears as a baseline in hypersonic-rANS.
found_via: Search result for htscodecs from WebSearch 'rANS entropy coder SIMD github ...'; opened repo page and BENCHMARKS.md via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: rans-tricks
workload: enwik8 encode and decode with adaptive-probability branchless rANS variants (4-way interleaved and implicit).
claimed_speedup: 4-way interleaved rans trick 415 MB/s encode, 460 MB/s decode vs 4-way interleaved standard rans 250 / 300 MB/s (about 1.66x / 1.53x, derived) and FSE 325 / 440 MB/s (about 1.28x / 1.05x, derived).
tradeoffs: Branchless adaptive rANS with no intrinsics or assembly (portable C++); only a small header (rans_byte.h), main.cpp and platform.h. Adaptive probabilities, so FSE (static tables) is not a like-for-like workload.
caveats: README says 'public domain, do whatever you want' but the repo shows no LICENSE file (only README.md, main.cpp, platform.h, rans_byte.h), so listed as reference (SPDX none); the author's statement would make it copyable if accepted. The FSE row (325 MB/s encode, 440 MB/s decode) is identical to the Proba80 FSE row in the FSE README, measured on an i7-5600U, so it was probably not measured on the Ryzen 1700; the FSE comparison is doubtful. No compiler or flags, tiny benchmark, last commit 2018.

name: TurboRC (Turbo-Range-Coder, TurboANX rANS)
baseline: unnamed 'next fastest range coder' and 'other adaptive ANS' in the README; the README's own tables compare only TurboRC variants (and bsc, bzip3, bzip2 for the BWT sections); the comparison page sites.google.com/site/powturbo/entropy-coder was not reachable
workload: Order-0/1/2 range coding, adaptive CDF rANS and bitwise coders on enwik8, enwik9 and enwik8 BWT output (100 MB); also a Silesia run.
claimed_speedup: README text: 'Up to 3 times faster than the next fastest range coder with similar compression ratio'; 'No other adaptive ANS encode or decode faster with better compression'. Table (enwik8bwt): order-0 rc 88.20 MB/s encode, 88.54 MB/s decode; 'ans auto' 116.76 / 202.27 MB/s; 'ans sse' 126.57 / 175.43 MB/s. No named competitor row for the range coder or ANS claims was seen.
compiler_and_flags: GCC >= 4.6 / Clang >= 3.2 listed as supported; benchmark flags not stated
stars_or_usage: 96 stars; TurboRC also feeds powturbo's TurboBench
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0 with a commercial licence on request; C with C++ headers; SSE/AVX2/NEON/RVV rANS paths; many predictors and a BWT pipeline included.
caveats: The README does not name the competing range coder or ANS implementation behind the 3x claim, so the baseline is unconfirmed; hence confidence is low. Hardware not stated in the README text opened. The BWT benchmark section (dated 2026-10) compares full BWT compressors, not entropy coders. The linked Entropy Coder Benchmark page was blocked. Numbers for FSE/Huffman are on that page and not verified here. Related TurboANX appears as a (closed-source) row in the hypersonic-rANS benchmark.
found_via: WebSearch 'github powturbo Turbo-Range-Coder TurboANX entropy coder benchmark'; github.com/topics/entropy-coding page

name: MULTIANS (massively parallel ANS decoding on GPUs)
baseline: multicore CPU tANS decoder included in the same repo (for comparison with the GPU decoder)
workload: Decoding of raw, unpartitioned tANS streams (256 symbols, exponentially distributed data sets of user-chosen size) on a CUDA GPU vs a multi-threaded CPU decoder.
hardware: CUDA GPU compute capability 3.0+ (specific model not stated in README)
tradeoffs: CUDA only, GNU/Linux; single table, radix b=2 (1 bit per renormalisation step), alphabet up to 256; includes only a basic single-state tANS encoder; multi-table/multi-state version left as future work.
caveats: Tier B only because it is a peer-reviewed conference paper (DOI 10.1145/3337821.3337888, linked in the README); the paper and the numbers were NOT opened (doi.org and dl.acm.org blocked), and the README carries no numbers, so claimed_speedup is null. The baseline is the repo's own CPU port, not a recognised incumbent such as FSE; treat as low confidence until a verifier reads the paper.
found_via: github.com/topics/ans?l=c%2B%2B page and WebSearch 'tANS GPU entropy coder github dietgpu ANS compression throughput'
